messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 79, Leonard was an African American man who had spent most of his adult life working in a warehouse, where the noise, movement, and steady routines had long felt easier to manage than being alone with his thoughts. He was divorced now and living with the quiet that came after years of marriage, but quiet was not something he welcomed. When he first came for help, he described a lifelong tendency to keep himself around other people, even when he did not especially want company, because being by himself left him vulnerable to memories he could not quite grasp yet could still feel in his body. He had built a way of getting through the day by staying busy, keeping conversations going, and, when that was not enough, drinking or using medication or drugs to dull the edge of what would otherwise rise up in him. He also knew, with some embarrassment, that he sometimes picked arguments or created drama just to shift the focus away from himself and whatever was stirring inside.

Leonard traced the beginning of all this back to childhood, to a home where domestic violence was a recurring and frightening part of life. He remembered being a boy and hearing a door slam hard enough to shake him, followed by shouting and the sound of adults moving with force through the house. The details did not come to him as a neat story. Even now, when he tried to explain what had happened, he said the memory was hard to reach deliberately, as if his mind could not bring up the scene in a complete way. What he had instead were disconnected pieces: the crack of a door opening or slamming, the sharp smell of alcohol on someone’s breath, the feel of standing outside or near the house in a natural setting while something awful unfolded inside. At times the fragments did not form pictures at all, only a full wave of fear and helplessness that arrived without warning. He would be standing in the warehouse, or sitting at home, and suddenly feel the same terror and dread he had felt as a child, even when he could not see the event clearly in his mind.

Certain moments in the present made those pieces more vivid. A door slamming in the warehouse, or the heavy roll-up door closing with a sharp bang, could make him jolt and look around before he was fully aware of why. The smell of alcohol was especially unsettling; if a coworker had been drinking the night before, or if he passed someone carrying alcohol at a family gathering, Leonard would tense and feel an immediate sense of unease. He also noticed that being in nature could be difficult when it resembled the outdoor spaces around the house where he had once stood as a child, listening from outside and waiting for the noise to stop. In parks or wooded areas, or even when the warehouse dock opened onto an expanse of trees and open ground, he sometimes felt pulled back into that old atmosphere of danger, as if the surroundings themselves were too similar to what he had known before.

Over the years, Leonard learned to arrange his life around these reactions without fully naming them. He kept himself surrounded by people because solitude gave the fragments room to surface. He drank or used substances when the feelings became too strong or when the day had left him stripped of his usual defenses. He stirred up conflict when he felt himself getting too inward, because upsetting someone else seemed, for a moment, more manageable than facing the memories that hovered just beneath awareness. These habits affected his relationships and made retirement impossible to imagine, so he stayed with work longer than he might have otherwise, relying on the warehouse environment to keep him occupied and near others. Even there, though, he had to navigate the occasional slam of a door, the smell of alcohol on a colleague, or the discomfort of being sent outdoors to check a shipment or wait near the loading area.

By the time he sought help, Leonard was worn down by how often the past could break in without a picture, arriving instead as bodily terror and scattered scraps he could not assemble. He was not asking to remember everything. What brought him in was the exhaustion of living around those moments, the strain on his relationships, and the fear that the same old reactions had narrowed his life more than he had admitted. At this stage, he hoped for some relief from the constant need to avoid being alone with himself, and he was most afraid that if he stopped drinking, stopped filling every silence, or stopped distracting himself with conflict, the full force of those childhood memories would come back all at once and leave him overwhelmed.
